specs.anchorText: OpenCV stores color as BGR; everyone else uses RGB. Display an OpenCV-loaded photo
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background, generous margins: three friendly cartoon paint-bucket characters labeled only by their colors, a red one, a green one, and a blue one, lining up to pour into a portrait frame. One library robot hands them over in red-green-blue order producing a natural rosy-cheeked smiling portrait, while a second slightly mischievous robot accidentally swaps the red and blue buckets, so the same portrait comes out with comically blue skin and an orange sky. The two portraits sit side by side for contrast. Friendly and approachable XKCD-inspired style, expressive characters, minimal clutter, suitable for a technical textbook. No text or lettering in the image. Gentle humor. One clear visual metaphor: swapped color order ruins a face.
specs.alt: Two side-by-side cartoon portraits: one painted with red, green, and blue buckets in the correct order looks natural, while the other has its red and blue buckets swapped and comes out with blue skin and an orange sky, illustrating the OpenCV BGR versus RGB channel-order trap that silently tints images.
specs.caption: Swap two channels and nobody crashes; the face just turns quietly, catastrophically blue. Channel-order bugs degrade aesthetics, not exit codes.

specs.anchorText: The single most common performance bug in imaging code is a per-pixel Python loop.
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background, generous margins: a tall friendly stepladder rising left to right, with cheerful cartoon worker robots on each rung carrying pixel blocks upward. On the lowest rung one exhausted robot slowly hands up pixels one by one (a tiny snail beside it for slowness); on higher rungs robots carry whole crates of pixels at once, then a robot with a tidy lookup card, and at the very top a fast glowing rocket-powered robot zips a giant stack of pixels in one motion. Each rung is progressively faster and the robots look happier and more energetic going up. Friendly XKCD-meets-Kurzgesagt style, expressive characters, minimal clutter, suitable for a technical textbook. No text or lettering in the image. One clear visual metaphor: climbing a performance ladder out of slow per-pixel work.
specs.alt: A stepladder of cartoon robots where the bottom rung moves pixels one at a time beside a snail, and higher rungs carry whole crates, then use a lookup card, then a rocket-powered robot moves a huge stack at once, illustrating the performance ladder from a slow per-pixel Python loop up to vectorized, lookup-table, and GPU-accelerated speed.
specs.caption: The fix for slow imaging code is never a cleverer loop; it is climbing one rung higher and getting the loop out of Python entirely.

specs.caption: The GPU lane is blazing fast once you are on it, but a single small job pays the transfer toll twice and arrives later than if it had taken the ordinary road.

specs.anchorText: Both are legitimate SSIMs; they are just different numbers.
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background, generous margins: two friendly cartoon judge robots scoring the very same painting on an easel, each holding up a scorecard with a different number, because each measures with a different-sized measuring window, one holding a small square frame, the other a larger soft-edged circular lens. They look earnest and equally confident, not arguing, just disagreeing politely. A small identical recipe card pinned between them shows the same formula to signal it is the same metric. Friendly XKCD-meets-Kurzgesagt style, expressive characters, minimal clutter, suitable for a technical textbook. No text or lettering in the image. Gentle humor. One clear visual metaphor: same formula, different settings, different score.
specs.alt: Two earnest cartoon judge robots score the same painting with different numbers because one measures through a small square window and the other through a larger soft circular lens, illustrating that the same SSIM formula yields different scores under different window-shape and statistics conventions, so the metric is code with parameters, not just math.
specs.caption: Same formula, different settings, different score: a metric is code with parameters, and protocol disagreement can masquerade as a real improvement.
